The README names that as one of three ways a flag can be set and do nothing, because `-fhardened` yields to any explicit `-fno-` by design. observations.notes: The guide's TL;DR addendum asks for -fexceptions only for multi-threaded C code using glibc's pthreads, where thread cancellation unwinds through C frames. On another C library the check still publishes what the compiler did, `off` included, because the macro is the compiler's and discriminates the same way there (measured on Alpine with musl); that `off` says the toolchain does not default to -fexceptions, not that the guide's ask is unmet. Whether musl's or a BSD's cancellation benefits from the flag is unmeasured. C polarity: in C++ the macro is on by default and -fno-exceptions removes it, so this reading holds for C only. The openssf-tldr profile does not pass the flag, by that profile's design (the TL;DR block it carries); the explicit profile measures it. Two other spellings reach the macro. On gcc 13 and later -fnon-call-exceptions implies -fexceptions, and both checks read it as such; on gcc 11 and on clang it does nothing in C. clang's -fexceptions -fignore-exceptions defines the macro and emits no table, so this check reads `on` where the flag's cleanup tables are gone: that form is one the macro cannot see and except-table-emitted can, and the macro reading is withheld beside it under macro-contradicted-by-artifact, the reason naming both. clang's -fexceptions -fsjlj-exceptions is a form this check cannot tell apart: the macro is defined, but the frames register with the SjLj unwinder, which the forced unwind of glibc's cancellation does not run. On x86_64 the table is emitted and except-table-emitted reads `on` too; on 32-bit ARM clang 19.1.7 puts the table in .text, as it does under -fdwarf-exceptions, no .ARM.extab is written, and since the selector reaches the control arms, which then carry no mark either, except-table-emitted reads `probe-invalid` (Raspbian 13 armv6, measured 2026-10-21). observations.notes: The guide sanctions UBSan in production in trap mode, -fsanitize=undefined -fsanitize-trap=undefined (gcc's spelling of the same is also -fsanitize-undefined-trap-on-error), since a trap needs no runtime library. The probe's function loads an array element through a pointer, shifts it and adds to it, so the sanitizer's null, alignment, bounds, pointer-overflow, shift and signed-integer-overflow checks each have something to trap on, and a trap configuration narrower than the whole sanitizer that covers any of them reads `on` too, but for clang's signed-overflow trap alone: clang's -ftrapv, with no sanitizer, emits the same trap with the same check number, so a function whose only traps are that one is `indeterminate` under clang, and so is -fsanitize-trap=signed-integer-overflow alone there. A second function holds a construct for every other group gcc and clang instrument in C without a call (integer-divide-by-zero, vla-bound, unreachable, builtin, bool, the float, nonnull and nullability groups, clang's implicit-conversion and unsigned groups), a third indexes a global array of known size through a pointer to its element type (gcc's object-size and clang's local-bounds, which size the object; not bounds, which reads the array type the cast hides and has its construct in the first function, so a local-bounds handler beside a bounds trap is seen rather than folded) and a fourth calls through a function pointer (clang's function), and the probe records whether the compiler reports an undefined-behavior group enabled, where the compiler answers __has_feature (clang, and gcc 16.1.1; gcc 13.3.0 answers nothing). `off` says no check traps in any of the four functions or gcc's .cold parts of them, no group the probe has no construct for is reported enabled, and the compile's own sanitizer words, read from the driver's -### command, name no group in trap mode: UBSan is in handler mode, or not enabled, and the default profiles enable it nowhere. The groups with no construct are enum and return, which neither compiler checks in C, and clang's object-size, which clang keeps only for a provable fault; any of them enabled in trap mode with no trap and no handler is `indeterminate`, under the compiler's report where it gives one and under the words everywhere (so gcc 13's -fsanitize=enum in handler mode reads `off`, its words naming no trapped group, where gcc 16 reports the group and reads `indeterminate`); so is an object without the construct functions; and one of them left in handler mode beside trapped groups is `indeterminate` under the same words, since the artifact's traps say nothing of that group. Under clang, -fsanitize=object-size at -O0 reads `off` because clang drops the group with a warning, which the observation's build.stderr carries: no check exists to run in either mode. clang's local-bounds traps by default and reads `on` with or without -fsanitize-trap naming it, beside -fsanitize-trap=undefined too, which leaves that default in place; -fno-sanitize-trap=local-bounds puts it in handler mode and reads `off` alone and `indeterminate` beside trapped groups, and clang's -fsanitize=bounds with no trap flag reads `indeterminate` the same way, since the bounds group includes local-bounds trapping beside array-bounds calling its handler. -fsanitize-trap=undefined without -fsanitize=undefined does nothing and reads `off`. A trap beside a runtime handler, which -fsanitize-trap=shift alone gives and which a construct-bearing group left in handler mode by -fno-sanitize-trap= gives, is `indeterminate`, and so is a trap beside any call in the first two functions, whatever the handler's name. Read from the code bytes of four functions in an object file, by a fixed-pattern search rather than a disassembler; `elf::code` says why that is sound for these functions and not for an arbitrary one, and why the third and fourth are searched for traps alone. A call in the function with neither a trap nor a handler is `indeterminate`, since the source calls nothing: clang's -ftrap-function=NAME, which turns each trap into a call to NAME (through a register under -mcmodel=large), reads so, and so do -fstack-protector-all, gcc's -ftrapv, -pg and -fsanitize=address, among others, which put a call there for their own reasons; the same calls beside a trap withhold an `on`.

observations.notes: The sibling `noexecstack` check asks whether a *flag* was passed; this asks what the linker does when nothing was. The distinction matters because the stack is executable if any input requires it, and an object carrying no `.note.GNU-stack` has historically been read as requiring it, so one unmarked object silently makes a whole binary's stack executable. binutils built with `--enable-default-execstack=no` reverses that assumption. This is the only compiler-visible effect of Gentoo's `sys-devel/binutils[hardened]`, and the reason the probe is assembly: gcc emits the note into every object it produces, so a C source can only measure what gcc asked for, never what the linker assumes in its absence.

A probe function missing from the object withholds the reading rather than counting as unprotected, so gcc's slim -flto object, which holds no code, is indeterminate, and clang's -flto bitcode is not ELF and is indeterminate too. A raised --param=ssp-buffer-size still reads basic, since plain -fstack-protector admits the alloca function at any threshold; how large the threshold is, is ssp-covers-small-arrays' question. gcc's -fstack-protector-explicit instruments only functions marked stack_protect, none here, and reads absent, where ssp-level reads partial at explicit from the macro, except on Ubuntu 22.04, whose gcc 11.4.0 adds -fstack-protector-strong after it and reads strong; clang rejects that flag. Verified at 12% with the flag and 100% without, on gcc and clang. Needs a bounded RLIMIT_STACK to size the allocation from; an unbounded or very small stack yields a declined probe rather than a guess, and so does a limit whose allocation does not fit below the frame (16 TiB and up on 4-level x86_64, about 256 MiB and up for i386 in compat mode, measured 2026-10-05). Needs no kernel-ownership gate (`needs_vm`): the verdict is the compiler's probing, and the kernel only supplies the fault, the same kernel for all three arms of a run. Linux (as above), FreeBSD and macOS fault at the stack limit, so an arm that probes reads about 12% and one that does not 100% (FreeBSD 15.1 clang 19.1.7, quoted from the fleet's reports; macOS 27.0.1 Homebrew gcc 16.2.0). Where the arms do not discriminate the check is `probe-invalid`: on OpenBSD 7.9 the driver ignores the flag, so the arms are one program, and a fault outside `MAP_STACK` memory arrives at the faulting instruction, which is no distance below the frame. So a kernel can leave this check without a verdict, but cannot make it read another one. gcc's `-fhardened` turns stack-clash protection on beside an explicit `-fno-stack-clash-protection`, in either order and with no `-Whardened` warning, where the stack protector, `_FORTIFY_SOURCE`, `-fcf-protection`, `-ftrivial-auto-var-init` and the linker's PIE, RELRO and `-z now` each yield to an explicit countermand and draw a `-Whardened` warning (checked on Fedora 44 gcc 16.1.1): an arm built with both reads about 12%. defect.summary: Learning where the image is mapped, which every code-reuse technique needs and which a fixed load address hands over for free.
An attacker-influenced format string; with %n it becomes an arbitrary write.
Overwriting a relocation table entry that stays writable after startup, redirecting a later call.
A write past the end of a heap allocation, corrupting adjacent chunk data or allocator metadata.
Arithmetic that wraps or is assumed not to, typically producing an undersized allocation or a bypassed bounds check.

The indirect-branch equivalent of ROP, chaining existing indirect jumps and calls. No check here observes enforcement of the forward edge (IBT, BTI), so this status is unknown in every report; the CET and BTI macros, markings and landing pads bearing on it are counted in verdict_counts as markings.
Loading code from a path an attacker can influence, via a search path baked into the binary or a dlopen that should not have been possible.

A null pointer dereference the optimizer created by deleting a check it was entitled to assume redundant (CVE-2009-1897). That deletion is what the one check bearing on this class keeps from happening; a dereference the source itself performs is outside every check here, and this status says nothing about it.

The compiler removed or altered code because it was entitled to assume an undefined behaviour could not occur, so the written source and the generated code disagree and nothing in the build says so. CVE-2009-1897 is the worked example: a null check the author wrote, deleted because an earlier dereference proved the pointer non-null.
Chaining existing return sequences to execute attacker-chosen behaviour without injecting code. No single CWE describes it.
A write past the end of a stack buffer, overwriting saved registers, the return address, or an adjacent local.
Growing the stack past its guard region into an adjacent mapping by allocating a frame larger than one page without touching it.
Executing data written to the stack, which requires the stack to be mapped executable.
Calling a function with no declaration in scope, so the compiler assumes a signature that may not match the definition.
Reading an automatic variable that was never assigned, disclosing whatever the frame last held. The disclosure primitive in the rsync chain (CVE-2024-12085).
